articles.title: Timing of vaccine-associated anaphylaxis and implications for post-vaccination observation period: A systematic review and Canadian surveillance data analysis.
articles.summary: PMID: 42981916. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129303. BackgroundThe post-vaccination observation period ensures the rapid identification and clinical management of immediate adverse events following immunization, including anaphylaxis. Recommended observation periods vary internationally. In Canada, a 15 min observation period is standard. This systematic review assesses the empirical basis for these recommendations and the potential impact of varying observation period durations.ObjectiveTo describe time to onset of anaphylaxis following immunization and provide an empirical basis to evaluate variable post-vaccination observation period durations.MethodsThis study combined mixed methods to capture the available evidence base. A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines searched Embase and MEDLINE from inception to March 6, 2023, for studies reporting time to onset of anaphylaxis within 30 min of vaccination. Anaphylaxis reports submitted to the Canadian Adverse Events Following Immunization Surveillance System (CAEFISS) were also analyzed.ResultsOf 44 studies reporting 1365 cases of anaphylaxis, 1229 (90%) had recorded onset time, of which 802 (65%) occurred within 30 min. Among cases with sufficient temporal detail (n = 305), 236 (77%) had onset within 15 min; of 113 cases with 5-min interval data, 61% had onset within 5 min. Findings were broadly consistent across COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 vaccines, age groups, and levels of diagnostic certainty. Among 2193 CAEFISS reports, the median onset time was 12 min; 78% (n = 1702) occurred within 30 min, 80% (n = 1363) of which occurred within 15 min, and 46% (n = 628) of those within 5 min. Results were similar across age groups and vaccine types.ConclusionsVaccine-associated anaphylaxis most commonly presents within 15 min of vaccination. A routine 15-min observation period would be expected to capture most (77-80%) events occurring within 30 min.

articles.title: Differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines for their children, and changes in vaccine hesitancy since the pandemic: A national cross-sectional comparative study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962460. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129300. BackgroundEvidence suggests the COVID-19 pandemic had heterogeneous and vaccine-specific effects on parental attitudes toward childhood vaccination. A decline in vaccine confidence has been noted in some settings, however even studies reporting stable or increased confidence suggest polarized attitudes with stronger pro- and anti-vaccine views emerging concurrently. We explored differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward childhood routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccination, and changes in attitudes since the pandemic.MethodsIn 2025 we conducted a cross-sectional national online survey of parents with children aged 0-17 years using a polling firm. Previously validated questions asked about parents' attitudes toward vaccination using the '5C' scale, capturing separate responses for routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines. We assessed changes in attitudes about routine vaccination over time by comparing 5C responses from two previous surveys conducted in 2020 and 2021. We calculated proportions and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).ResultsRespondents (N = 1327) were proportionally representative across provinces, but not the territories. Parents were most confident in the safety of routine vaccines (71.0%, 95%CI 66.5-75.7), compared to influenza (63.7%, 95%CI 59.5-68.1) and COVID-19 (57.9%, 95%CI 53.9-62.1). The majority indicated the pandemic did not change attitudes about routine (60.8%) or influenza (63.7%) vaccination, while more than one-quarter (31.6% and 27.8%) reported that routine and influenza vaccines were more important following the pandemic. In 2025, a slightly higher proportion of parents reported low confidence in the safety and effectiveness of routine vaccines (12.7% and 9.2%, respectively), compared to 2021 (8.5% and 5.6%), and 2020 (12.2% and 6.8%).ConclusionsParental attitudes toward childhood COVID-19 vaccination differed from attitudes toward routine and influenza. Most parents reported positive or neutral impact of the pandemic on perceived importance of routine and influenza vaccines. Parents reported the highest positive attitudes toward routine vaccination mid-pandemic (2021), and parents' attitudes in 2025 were slightly less positive than in 2020 and 2021.

articles.title: Making inferences with incomplete epidemiological data: a proof-of-concept estimating measles vaccine coverage across Canada.
articles.summary: PMID: 42966042. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129261. Background & aims of studyCurrent measles outbreaks around the world have highlighted the evolving immunity landscape of some vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs). In Canada, there have been approximately 1,100 reported measles cases between January and June 2026 alone. This far exceeds the previous average annual case counts of <200. This significant outbreak has underscored the need to better understand the present state of population immunity to measles in Canada, an essential input parameter for outbreak response models. Most population immunity in this setting is derived from routine childhood vaccination, but vaccine coverage data is available heterogeneously across the country and is typically collected cross-sectionally to monitor population adherence to immunization schedules rather than to inform population-level susceptibility. This study developed statistical methods to adapt available measles vaccine coverage estimates into more complete estimates of present-day immunity in Canada by age and province/territory (PT).Methods & resultsFirst, a standardized dataset for vaccine coverage by PT was collated from existing publicly-available datasets and reports. A significant number of vaccine coverage estimates were missing by PT, dose, and year. We used Gaussian Process models to impute current coverage with at least one dose of a measles vaccine, to create a complete 'modelled dataset' by PT and age. Our modelling framework was tested against data for England, which was much more complete, to validate our approach.ImplicationsWe developed methodology for estimating vaccine coverage in the absence of detailed population immunity data, to support ongoing measles outbreak modelling response work. While this project focused on measles, we built the associated code/tools such that the methodology can be applied to other vaccine-preventable diseases in future outbreak settings.

articles.title: Changes in self-reported Long COVID in different variant-dominant phases of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic: the influence of vaccination on a diverse Israeli cohort study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42976511. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129308. Purpose of researchLong COVID (LC) risk varies across SARS-CoV-2 variants, but causal inference is complicated by rising vaccine coverage coinciding with viral evolution. We examined how pre-infection vaccination status modified LC risk across different pandemic periods dominated by different variants, to disentangle the contributions of viral evolution and vaccine-induced immunity. In this prospective cohort study of Israeli adults with SARS-CoV-2 infections from July 2021-March 2023, participants completed baseline and follow-up online surveys ≥60 days post-infection. LC was defined as ≥3 symptoms within validated symptom clusters. Infections were assigned to an infection period corresponding to the predominant circulating variant (Wild type, Alpha, Delta, Omicron) at onset time. Pre-infection vaccination was categorized as unvaccinated (0-1 doses), partially vaccinated (2 doses), or fully vaccinated (≥3 doses). Generalized estimating equations estimated multivariable risk ratios, adjusted for age, sex, and follow-up time. Among 1715 participants reporting 2018 infections, LC was reported following 30·4% of infections. In models adjusted for vaccination, LC risk did not differ between the Delta and Omicron-dominant periods (aRR 1·01, 95% CI 0·80-1·26). Among partially vaccinated individuals, infections during the Omicron-dominant period carried lower LC risk than during Delta (aRR 0·62, 95% CI 0·40-0·98). LC risk did not differ by variant-dominant periods among unvaccinated or fully vaccinated individuals.Major conclusionsObserved differences in LC risk at various periods of the pandemic dominated by different variants may be largely explained by concurrent increases in vaccine coverage rather than intrinsic changes in variant pathogenicity. Full pre-infection vaccination conferred consistent protection against LC regardless of the period of variant dominance.

articles.title: Outcome-related nonresponse bias, not systematic misreporting, explains overestimation of vaccine uptake in COVID-19 surveys.
articles.summary: PMID: 42967370. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129315. Authorities increasingly rely on surveys to generate real-time evidence on population behavior during epidemics, yet the reliability of such evidence is debated. We combine data from a large-scale Danish survey (n = 393,375; 50.42% women; mean age 49.46) conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic with individual-level administrative registries to identify sources of error in survey-based estimates of vaccine uptake. Comparing survey responses and actual vaccine uptake, we find no evidence of systematic overreporting. We evaluate nonresponse bias by comparing actual vaccination behavior among respondents with the full pool of 1.68 million invitees. Despite weighting for sociodemographic characteristics, respondents are 5.99 percentage points more likely to initiate vaccination and 12.91 percentage points more likely to receive a booster than the invited sample. These results indicate that outcome-related nonresponse bias-not misreporting-is the dominant source of survey error, implying that even weighted estimates may overstate vaccine uptake during epidemics.

articles.title: Rationale and design of randomized, double-blind trial evaluating the efficacy of single-dose HPV vaccine efficacy in women aged 18 to 30: The PRISMA trial.
articles.summary: PMID: 42976512. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129236. Evidence from the Costa Rica HPV Vaccine Trial suggested that a single dose may provide durable protection in young adult women. Subsequent studies confirmed the non-inferiority of one vs. two doses of the main vaccines among young girls. Vaccination of older cohorts might accelerate cervical cancer elimination, especially if a single dose provides adequate protection. Randomized data are needed to support extended-age, single-dose vaccination strategies. Herein, we present the design, rationale and recruitment results of a three-arm, randomized, double-blinded, clinical trial in Costa Rica to evaluate the efficacy of a single dose of the bivalent (Cervarix®) and nonavalent (Gardasil 9®) HPV vaccines compared with an active control (Tdap). 4925 HPV vaccine-naïve women aged 18-30 years old were enrolled, randomized 1:1:1, and followed for 36 months with cervicovaginal self-sampling every six months starting at 12 months, annual blood collection, and oral/anal sampling at selected visits, with high participation rates. Participants attended ~90% of planned study visits and >96% of attendees provided the necessary specimens. The primary endpoint is incident cerviccovaginal HPV16/18 infection persisting ≥6 months among women HPV16/18 DNA-negative at the enrollment and vaccination visits. Secondary endpoints include vaccine efficacy in the intention-to-treat cohort, oral and anal HPV16/18 protection, and immunogenicity profiles. Trial results will inform mathematical models estimating impact and cost-effectiveness of extending single-dose vaccination to adult young women and directly inform policy to enable extended-age, single-dose strategies to accelerate cervical cancer prevention globally. Furthermore, the study will provide the first evidence for single-dose efficacy against anal and oral HPV infection.

articles.title: Clinical endpoints for trials of Strep A vaccines: report of two expert meetings.
articles.summary: PMID: 42976510. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129262. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus; Strep A) causes a broad spectrum of diseases ranging from pharyngitis and skin infections to invasive disease and immune-mediated complications including acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and rheumatic heart disease (RHD). RHD remains one of the most important causes of cardiovascular mortality in young people globally, affecting more than 55 million individuals and causing over 370,000 deaths annually, predominantly in low- and middle-income countries. Despite this substantial burden, no licensed Strep A vaccine exists. A critical barrier to vaccine development is that there are many potential clinical trial endpoints capable of supporting regulatory approval while demonstrating meaningful public health impact. However, research gaps remain before these can be fully realised. To address this challenge, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Strep A Vaccine Global Consortium (SAVAC) convened two international expert consultations in London (September 2024) and Geneva (October 2025). Participants reviewed emerging scientific evidence, epidemiology, and regulatory considerations to define potential clinical development pathways and priority endpoints for Strep A vaccines. Consensus emerged that prevention of Strep A pharyngitis in children represents a feasible primary endpoint for initial proof-of-efficacy trials and potential licensure. Impetigo in children was recognized as an important endpoint, particularly in high-burden settings or where it contributes substantially to transmission and severe invasive infections or progression to RHD. Although prevention of RHD and invasive disease is the ultimate public health objective, advanced RHD was considered infeasible as a pre-licensure endpoint. Early RHD detected by echocardiography was identified as a promising intermediate outcome, but further epidemiological and validation studies could increase confidence in its use in pivotal trials. A clinical development pathway is proposed in which initial licensure is supported by efficacy against pharyngitis and possibly impetigo or early RHD with further evaluation of other severe outcomes such as invasive infections through large-scale trials and post-licensure studies. This pathway informs updates to the WHO Preferred Product Characteristics and Research and Development Roadmap and provides a coordinated strategy to accelerate the development and equitable global introduction of Strep A vaccines.
articles.normalizedTitle: Clinical endpoints for trials of Strep A vaccines: report of two expert meetings.

articles.title: Pneumococcal vaccine after hematopoietic cell transplantation: a rapid review of four-dose pneumococcal conjugate vaccine schedules.
articles.summary: PMID: 42966040. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129299. Hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) recipients are at substantially elevated risk for invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) due to prolonged immunocompromised state, yet optimal pneumococcal vaccine product selection and scheduling, including the role of higher-valency pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs), have not undergone Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices review. We conducted a rapid review to synthesize evidence on the immunogenicity and safety of four-dose PCV schedules in HCT recipients to inform future clinical guidance. Following Cochrane rapid review methods and PRISMA guidelines, we searched Medline, Embase, and Scopus (initial: November 2024; updated: March 2025) and identified 31 eligible studies. Four studies directly evaluated four-dose PCV13 or PCV15 regimens in allogeneic HCT recipients, and only one study provided a direct randomized comparison. Among studies that allowed comparison, four-dose PCV13 schedules consistently generated higher overall and serotype-specific IgG and opsonophagocytic activity responses than three-dose PCV13 followed by 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), while PPSV23 provided limited additional benefit when administered within 1-2 months of the final PCV13 dose. Both randomized and nonrandomized studies demonstrated robust antibody responses following the fourth PCV dose, and safety profiles were acceptable. Although adverse events were more frequent after the fourth PCV dose, serious vaccine-related events were rare and difficult to attribute given underlying comorbidities. Findings from 27 supporting studies further contextualized optimal timing and product choice, showing that later initiation (≥6 months post-HCT) was often associated with stronger and more durable immune responses, although waning immunity remained common. PCV-based regimens were consistently more immunogenic than PPSV23-only schedules. No studies evaluated PCV20 or PCV21 in HCT recipients, representing a major evidence gap despite their expanded serotype coverage. Overall, the available evidence provides evidence of immunogenicity and safety with a four-dose PCV-based schedule initiated 3-6 months post-HCT, while critical research gaps remain regarding higher-valency PCVs, mixed-product schedules, and strategies tailored to transplant type or individual immunologic risk.

articles.title: Investigating predictors of pertussis vaccination in pregnancy across England: cross sectional studies of maternity staff and mothers.
articles.summary: PMID: 42987448. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129309. IntroductionPertussis vaccination is recommended for all pregnant women in England. Uptake remains suboptimal, with regional and demographic variability, leaving neonates at risk. This persists despite expansion of vaccine provision across maternity services since 2017. This study aimed to identify determinants of inequity and opportunities for intervention.MethodsCross-sectional online surveys of: ii) 551 maternity healthcare professionals (HCPs), comparing those working in trusts within the highest- and lowest-vaccinating regions of England. i) 377 mothers of young babies from lowest-vaccinating regions, comparing women vaccinated versus unvaccinated against pertussis in their recent pregnancy; and Questionnaires were informed by the COM-B framework. Logistic regression modelling assessed factors associated with vaccination, alongside content analysis of free-text responses.Resultsi) HCP survey: Area-level deprivation was strongly associated with low-vaccinating regions. Controlling for this, low-vaccinating regions were associated with HCPs' lower confidence in vaccine discussions and more perceiving these as burdensome, greater desire for training, and increased perceived responsibility for vaccination. Free-text responses described midwifery culture of providing vaccination information neutrally, avoiding direct recommendations in favour of supporting women's choice. ii) Mothers' survey: Most mothers (90%) rated HCPs as influential in their vaccination decision. Non-vaccination (20% of sample) was most strongly associated with lack of awareness that pertussis vaccination was recommended and lack of conviction that their midwife supported vaccination. Main reasons for vaccination were safety for the baby and HCP recommendation. Clear midwife recommendation was associated with satisfactory perceptions of vaccine communication across groups. The importance of access was commonly recognised but did not differentiate between groups in either study.ConclusionsMidwives need support to avoid a neutral stance and provide clear, confident recommendations, including infant safety reassurance. Funding models should account for deprivation, not solely service size, to help reduce vaccination inequity.

articles.title: An open label, uncontrolled clinical trial of immunogenicity and safety of yellow fever vaccine in adults with chronic kidney disease as compared to immunocompetent.
articles.summary: PMID: 42971112. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129314. IntroductionDuring a yellow fever (YF) epidemic in Brazil, vaccination campaigns targeting the entire population in the affected areas were conducted, bringing up an opportunity to prospectively evaluate YF vaccine's immunogenicity and safety in adults with chronic kidney disease (CKD).MethodsOpen-label, uncontrolled clinical trial involving adults aged ≥18 years with CKD on dialysis (CKD-D) or not (CKD-ND) and immunocompetent, who had denied previous YF vaccination. All of them received a YF vaccine standard dose (0.5 mL). Neutralizing antibodies were measured by microneutralization test with 50% reduction of lysis plaques (micro-PRN50) 10, 30 and 365 days after vaccination. Viremia was evaluated by RT-PCR. Adverse events following immunization (AEFI) were monitored. Primary outcomes were seropositivity and seroconversion rates. Secondary outcomes were antibody geometric mean titers (GMT) and safety.Results154 participants were included: 54 CKD-D, 41 CKD-ND and 59 immunocompetent. Median age was 50, 61 and 47 years, respectively. Ten days after vaccination (D10), seropositivity was significantly lower in CKD (CKD-ND, 62.5%; CKD-D, 48%) than in immunocompetent (86.7%) and CKD had lower GMT. On D30, GMT increased in all groups, without significant differences on seropositivity and GMT between groups. On D365, GMT decreased, but most participants persisted seropositive, without significant differences. On D10, viremia was detected in 28.8% of CKD-D; 32.3% of CKD-ND, and 28.9% of immunocompetent, without significant difference between groups. The CKD participants had lower viremia. Immunocompetent participants more frequently reported AEFI (66.7%) than CKD-ND (48.5%) and CKD-D (48.8%). Most common AEFI were headache (32.7%), myalgia (28.4%) and injection site pain (25.3%).ConclusionsAdults with CKD had a robust although delayed neutralizing antibody response to YF vaccine and the vaccine was well-tolerated. The small sample size precluded the detection of small differences in immune response between the groups and the occurrence of rare serious AEFI related to YF vaccine.

articles.title: Exploring perceptions of 4CMenB vaccination for gonorrhoea prevention among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and healthcare professionals in England: a qualitative focus group study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962461. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129232. BackgroundIn November 2023, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation advised the UK government to introduce a targeted, opportunistic vaccination programme using 4CMenB in sexual health services to prevent gonorrhoea primarily in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) at higher risk of infection. Evidence on4CMenB vaccination acceptability was required.MethodsThree focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted with 17 GBMSM aged ≥18 years, resident in England, who self-reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection or ≥ 5 sexual partners in the previous 12-months, alongside one FGD with five sexual healthcare professionals (HCPs). Data were analysed using thematic analysis and organised and interpreted using the Vaccine Uptake Continuum and the Social Ecological Model.ResultsParticipating GBMSM and HCPs generally expressed positive perceptions of 4CMenB vaccination. GBMSM described vaccination as supporting sexual wellbeing and reducing anxiety about gonorrhoea. While the estimated effectiveness (30-35%) was perceived as modest, it did not deter acceptability but reduced willingness to actively seek vaccination. Structural constraints (e.g. limited appointment availability) and restrictive eligibility criteria were identified as barriers to equitable uptake. Community-based delivery models were supported as a potential approach to improve access. HCPs drew on mpox vaccination experience to anticipate implementation challenges and emphasised clear guidance and sustainable resourcing. Additional protection against meningitis was generally a secondary influence.Conclusions4CMenB vaccination for gonorrhoea was acceptable to participating GBMSM and HCPs; however, uptake is likely to depend on ease of access, clear communication, and system-level support. Addressing structural constraints and supporting community-based delivery may help achieve equitable delivery of 4CMenB.

articles.title: Temporal changes in incidence of Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration (SIRVA) after COVID-19 vaccination.
articles.summary: PMID: 42966041. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129304. BackgroundShoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration (SIRVA) is a rare but potentially preventable adverse event associated with improper intramuscular (IM) injections into the deltoid muscle. This study aimed to assess temporal changes in SIRVA incidence following universal COVID-19 vaccination in Japan and to examine the associations with sex, age, and vaccine type.MethodsWe analyzed publicly available passive adverse event reports from the Health Science Council in Japan between 2/17/2021 and 3/12/2023. Two SIRVA criteria (broad and narrow) were used. SIRVA cases per 1,000,000 doses and rate ratios were calculated across 9 three-month intervals. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to sex, age, and vaccine type (Pfizer or Moderna).ResultsAmong the 433,538,539 vaccine doses administered, 574 (broad) and 76 (narrow) SIRVA cases were identified. The highest estimated three-month reporting incidence was 22.96 cases per 1,000,000 doses administered. The incidence of SIRVA declined over time, especially between the first and second three-month intervals. According to both criteria, the reporting incidence was twice as high in women. The highest reporting incidence was observed in individuals aged 35-39 (broad) and 60-64 years (narrow). No significant differences in SIRVA incidence were observed between the vaccine types.ConclusionThe temporal decline in SIRVA incidence may reflect improvements in the IM injection technique during the COVID-19 mass vaccination, but other factors including changes in reporting behavior should also be considered. Training in proper IM injection techniques, monitoring adverse events, and raising awareness of SIRVA are important to further reduce the incidence of SIRVA.

articles.title: Exercise and vaccine immune response: A scoping review exploring the underlying immunological mechanisms.
articles.summary: PMID: 42966038. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129302. IntroductionThe precise mechanisms by which exercise modulates the immune response to vaccination remain largely unelucidated in the existing literature. This scoping review aims to compile and critically analyse the available evidence pertaining to the underlying mechanisms responsible for the enhancing effect of exercise on vaccine-induced immunity.MethodsThe study was planned in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive and structured scoping review of the literature was conducted to investigate the effect of exercise on vaccine immune response. Three key electronic databases-PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar-were systematically searched for relevant studies published from January 1, 1990, to June 30, 2025. Strict inclusion and exclusion criteria were established and rigorously applied to the identified studies. Both animal and human studies were included to ensure a broad and comprehensive assessment of all proposed mechanisms.ResultsThe initial literature search yielded 4314 study titles, from which 199 papers were identified as potentially relevant and subsequently subjected to abstract-level examination. Following this screening, 38 studies met the predefined inclusion criteria and were incorporated into this review, comprising 26 human studies (68.42%) and 12 animal studies. The publication dates of the included studies ranged from 1999 to 2025. Overall, 14 distinct mechanisms were identified as potential explanations for the observed effect of exercise on vaccine immune response.ConclusionThe most compelling mechanisms identified in this review for exercise's enhancing effect on vaccine immune response include: upregulated Interleukin-6 (IL-6) expression, enhanced Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) expression, immune stimulation resulting from myocyte damage, prolonged antibody persistence, and enhanced immune cell metabolic efficiency in physically active individuals. This review highlights the critical need to identify the optimal "golden zone" of exercise intensity and to further elucidate sex-related dimorphisms to maximise clinical efficacy.

articles.title: A qualitative examination of factors impacting Black and Latino sexual minority men's vaccination decision-making and experiences: application of the stages of vaccine readiness and action theoretical framework.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962463. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129283. BackgroundBlack and Latino sexual minority men (BLSMM) experience persistent inequities in vaccine uptake, driven by structural barriers, medical mistrust, misinformation, and limited culturally responsive communication. This study applied the Stages of Vaccine Readiness and Action (SVRA) framework to examine vaccine decision-making among BLSMM during infectious disease outbreaks in the United States.MethodsWe conducted a qualitative interpretative phenomenological study using semi-structured interviews with 41 BLSMM in California and New York between August 2021 and December 2022. Interviews explored vaccine experiences and barriers and facilitators to uptake. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis guided by the SVRA framework.ResultsParticipants ranged from 19 to 65 years; 73% identified as Black and 93% as male. Vaccine decision-making was dynamic and shaped by individual and structural factors across five SVRA stages: skepticism, curiosity, readiness, action, and maintenance. Skepticism reflected medical mistrust, misinformation, safety concerns, and distrust of governmental and scientific institutions. Curiosity centered on vaccine development, side effects, and conflicting information. Readiness and action were facilitated by trusted healthcare providers, protecting oneself and others, chronic health conditions, and community-based vaccination. Transportation, appointment systems, employment demands, and healthcare access impeded vaccination. Maintenance was undermined by vaccine fatigue, booster burden, side-effect concerns, and changing perceptions of vaccine effectiveness.ConclusionVaccine decision-making among BLSMM occurs along a continuum shaped by psychosocial and structural determinants. Findings support culturally responsive education, trust-building, community-engaged interventions, and structural supports. Similar barriers may affect uptake and sustained engagement with long-acting injectable HIV prevention and treatment modalities.

articles.title: Childhood vaccination in Mali: Determinants and differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions from the 2023-2024 Demographic and Health Survey.
articles.summary: PMID: 42971113. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129275. BackgroundArmed conflict may disrupt immunization services and increase barriers to childhood vaccination. This study examined determinants of full basic childhood vaccination in Mali and assessed whether they differed between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions.MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of the 2023-2024 Mali Demographic and Health Survey, including 2859 children aged 12-23 months. Full basic vaccination was defined as receipt of Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccine, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of oral polio vaccine (excluding the birth dose), and measles vaccine. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were fitted nationally and separately for conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. Interactions between conflict status and selected explanatory variables were tested.ResultsFull basic vaccination coverage was 51.87%. Coverage did not differ significantly between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions (50.08% vs 52.64%; p = 0.467), and conflict status was not independently associated with vaccination after adjustment. Antenatal care attendance and facility-based delivery were consistently associated with higher odds of full vaccination. In conflict-affected regions, media exposure and shorter perceived distance to health facilities were also associated with higher vaccination uptake. A significant interaction was observed between conflict status and distance to health facility (p = 0.01).ConclusionsChildhood vaccination coverage in Mali remains suboptimal. Although overall coverage was similar across conflict and non-conflict regions, determinants differed by context, highlighting the need for tailored strategies to improve vaccine uptake.

articles.title: Impact of single-dose universal varicella vaccination program on paediatric varicella-zoster virus-related hospitalisations in Australia, 2002-2022.
articles.summary: PMID: 42971114. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129274. BackgroundAustralia introduced a single-dose varicella vaccine at 18 months of age on the National Immunisation Program in 2005. With this study, we aimed to assess the long-term impact of this program on paediatric varicella and zoster hospitalisations and complications, and to describe trends in immunocompromising conditions among hospitalised cases.MethodsWe obtained hospitalisations among children aged <15 years with a varicella (B01) or zoster (B02) ICD-10-AM code during 2002-2022 from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare National Hospital Morbidity Database. Following a literature review, we identified hospitalisations with varicella- or zoster-related complication code(s), and hospitalisations with concurrent code(s) indicating immunocompromise. We calculated hospitalisation rates, rate ratios, and the proportion of hospitalisations with complication or concurrent code for immunocompromise, by age group.FindingsImmediately following introduction of the varicella vaccination program, paediatric varicella hospitalisation rates rapidly declined, with a subsequent more gradual decline. In the 2015-2019 period, varicella hospitalisation rates were 81%, 94%, 88% and 70% lower than the 2002-2005 rates in the age groups <18 months, 18-59 months, 5-9 years and 10-14 years, respectively. Zoster hospitalisation rates declined over the study period in the age groups 18 months-14 years of age. There was a reduction in the rates of varicella and zoster hospitalisations with complication. The proportion of varicella hospitalisations with coded immunocompromising condition increased, though the absolute number of such hospitalisations decreased, whereas this proportion (and absolute number) decreased for zoster hospitalisations.DiscussionA substantial reduction in the burden of paediatric varicella and zoster was observed following introduction of Australia's single-dose varicella vaccination program. However, vulnerable populations remain and strategies to improve protection of particularly children <18 months of age and immunocompromised individuals, should be explored.

articles.title: Adult immunization program infrastructure and vaccine access across state, local, and territorial immunization programs, United States, 202425.
articles.summary: PMID: 42981915. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129297. BackgroundIn the United States, adult vaccination coverage is low, contributing to high rates of vaccine-preventable diseases. State, local, and territorial health departments ('jurisdictions') use federal funding to support adult immunization programs, manage outbreaks, and provide vaccines to eligible adults. We identified five core adult immunization program components for a jurisdiction to be considered a robust program. We evaluated implementation of five core components of jurisdiction adult immunization programs and perceived success in providing vaccine access.MethodsWe surveyed 64 CDC-funded jurisdictions on adult program operations and perceived success in vaccine access.ResultsVariability in implementing core components was observed across jurisdictions, from 5% implementing none to 5% implementing all five and 90% implementing between one and four. Nineteen jurisdictions reported high perceived success in providing vaccine access.ConclusionThis study highlights substantial variability in adult immunization program infrastructure and identifies funding diversification as a promising area to improve vaccine access.

articles.title: Ethical concerns of vaccine hesitant Canadians.
articles.summary: PMID: 42971109. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129311. BackgroundVaccine hesitancy persists across Canada. Research on vaccine hesitancy has tended to overlook the contribution of distinctly ethical concerns regarding vaccines and vaccine policies, despite their prominence in societal debates concerning vaccination. This study begins to fill the gap of understanding the ethical concerns of vaccine hesitant individuals.MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted with twelve participants from across Canada. Our study was guided by Betsch's 5 antecedents to vaccination and Giubilini's ethics of vaccination.ResultsFive themes that describe participants' ethical concerns were generated: freedom, consent, motivations of pharmaceutical companies, what is owed to others, recognition of terminology as 'ethical. Participants demonstrated variation and gaps in understanding of ethical concepts and terminology as they relate to vaccination, despite expressing concerns of an ethical nature.DiscussionThree themes of our study align with Betsch's framework: Consent = Constraints, Pharmaceutical Concerns = Confidence, and What is Owed to Others = Collective Responsibility. There is opportunity for further research exploring the ethical concerns of vaccine hesitant individuals framed as Choice that explores consent and vaccine policies that are not explicitly described in other vaccine hesitancy frameworks.ConclusionThis is the first study in Canada that explores the distinctly ethical concerns of vaccine hesitant individuals. Freedom, consent, motivations of pharmaceutical companies, and what is owed to others were identified as ethical issues related to vaccine hesitancy.

articles.title: Candida albicans vaccines: from cell wall architecture to protective immunity.
articles.summary: PMID: 42967371. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129312. Candida albicans is an opportunistic fungal pathogen that colonizes the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vaginal mucosa. Immunosuppression or increased fungal virulence permits extensive mucosal replication and tissue invasion, driving either recurrent superficial infection or life-threatening systemic disease. Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is predominantly caused by. It substantially impairs quality of life in women of reproductive age. Although azoles such as fluconazole are effective, emerging resistance and frequent recurrence limit their long-term utility. These constraints highlight the urgent need for preventive strategies against VVC. This review summarizes the landscape of cell wall antigens and their immunobiology, identifies key translational barriers, and proposes targeted strategies to advance next-generation antifungal vaccines, thereby providing a reference for future vaccine development.

articles.title: Maternal history of child marriage, educational attainment, and children's vaccination: Evidence from the Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey, 2017.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962462. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129271. IntroductionChild marriage, i.e., first cohabitating before 18 years of age, is a critical social issue that could affect a women's educational attainment, their own health, and their child's health. This study investigated the association between maternal history of child marriage and childhood vaccination rates in Indonesia, and analyzed whether maternal education was an effect modifier of this relationship.MethodsThis study analyzed the 2017 Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey, a nationally representative cross-sectional survey. Maternal history of child marriage was assessed as the main exposure, full childhood vaccination as the outcome, and maternal completion of high school as the potential effect modifier. Robust Poisson regression was used to examine the association between maternal history of child marriage and full childhood vaccination, adjusted for maternal, paternal, household, and child-related factors.ResultsOverall, among 7785 mothers, 22.1% had a history of child marriage, and 64.9% of children were fully vaccinated. Full vaccination was 56.1% among mothers with a history of child marriage, compared to 67.4% among mothers without. In an adjusted model, mothers with a history of child marriage had 0.86 (95% CI: 0.81, 0.91) times the prevalence of fully vaccinating their children compared to mothers without this history. There was a non-significant trend (P = 0.253) between maternal education and history of child marriage, with vaccination highest in those with no child marriage and a high school education (71.3%), and lowest in those with a history of child marriage and no high school education (54.8%).ConclusionsMothers with a history of child marriage are more likely to not vaccinate their children. This study emphasizes a critical need for public health and socioeconomic interventions to prevent child marriage and increase children's vaccination rates in households whose mothers have had a history of child marriage.
